analysis.one_liner: Removes the century-old liability cap that limits what shipping companies must pay victims of fires at sea.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced after the Deepwater Horizon disaster, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a shipping law dating to the 1800s, a shipowner whose vessel catches fire can limit what it owes victims — including the families of workers who die — to roughly the value of the vessel plus pending freight. This bill would repeal those limits for deaths, injuries, and lost cargo from fires on seagoing vessels. It was introduced two months after the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion in the Gulf of Mexico, and its effective date was written to apply retroactively to April 15, 2010 — before that disaster. The bill went to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Seafarers, passengers, and the families of people killed in shipboard fires, plus cargo owners whose goods are destroyed — they could pursue full compensation from shipowners instead of a payout capped by the value of the vessel. Crew members, who are injured and killed in maritime fires far more often than the general public, would be the main human beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the provisions of the Limitation of Liability Act that let shipowners cap what they must pay for personal injury, death, or lost merchandise in fire cases on seagoing vessels.
Victims and their families would be able to pursue full compensation in court instead of a share of a capped fund based on the vessel's value.
Full liability would give shipowners a stronger financial incentive to invest in fire safety, crew training, and equipment, since they could no longer limit their downside after a disaster.

analysis.who_pays: Shipping companies, offshore drilling contractors, and their insurers, who would face potentially unlimited damages for fire-related deaths, injuries, and lost cargo instead of a cap tied to the vessel's value. Some of that cost would flow into insurance premiums and freight rates.

drawbacks.text: The repeal took effect retroactively, as if enacted on April 15, 2010 — weeks before the bill was introduced — exposing companies to unlimited liability for incidents that had already happened under the old rules.

Shipping is a capital-intensive, thin-margin business; removing liability caps entirely can raise insurance and operating costs that get passed through freight rates to the prices consumers pay for imported goods.

Liability caps exist in maritime law partly so that a single catastrophic accident cannot bankrupt an owner before all victims are paid; full uncapped liability shifts all of that risk onto shipowners and, through them, their insurers, which some argue can complicate and slow compensation in mass-casualty cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real: families who lost people and businesses that lost property in a major fire at sea would have had a full shot at compensation instead of a payment capped by century-old law, and full liability would give shipping companies a stronger financial reason to invest in safety. The drawbacks are serious, though. Making the repeal retroactive to three weeks before enactment raises fair-notice concerns — companies would face new, unlimited liability for a disaster that happened before the law changed — and shipping is a business where a single catastrophic fire can exceed what one company can pay, which is why some form of liability limit exists in many countries. An honest supporter would acknowledge that completely uncapped liability could raise insurance costs and freight prices, and that courts might struggle with the retroactive application. A narrower fix targeting the specific gap exposed by the 2010 disaster might have had a better chance of passage.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never voted on it, and the two-year Congress ran out with the bill still stuck there.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the RESTORE Act on June 10, 2010, with Senators Leahy and Whitehouse, two months after the Deepwater Horizon rig exploded and burned in the Gulf of Mexico.
The bill would repeal sections of the Limitation of Liability Act that let shipowners cap their payments for deaths, injuries, and lost merchandise from fires at sea.
The repeal was written to take effect retroactively, as of April 15, 2010 — about two months before the bill was introduced and before the bill's enactment.
On the day of introduction the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a markup or voted, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shipping companies, offshore drilling contractors, and their insurers kept the old liability caps that limit what they owe victims of fires at sea; victims and their families remained dependent on whatever compensation those caps and separate arrangements allowed.

against.name: Ocean shipping and maritime industry interests
against.role: Vessel owners, drilling contractors, and marine insurers
against.what_they_did: Opposed losing the Limitation of Liability Act's cap, which limits their payout for deaths, injuries, and cargo losses from fires at sea to roughly the vessel's value.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its referral on June 10, 2010, never scheduling a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and the bill's four cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would strip shipowners of the century-old right to cap their payout for fire-related deaths, injuries, and lost cargo at roughly the vessel's value, exposing them to unlimited damages. Cargo owners and crews would gain full compensation; the cost falls on vessel owners and their insurers.
Uncapped liability for fire losses means potentially unlimited payouts, which insurers would have to price into premiums. Those costs eventually flow into freight rates and consumer prices.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling contractors and oil companies
industries.note: The bill was introduced in the immediate aftermath of the Deepwater Horizon disaster, and the effective date was set to reach that incident. Removing liability limits narrows an escape hatch that rig and platform owners have used to shrink their exposure after catastrophic accidents at sea.
